article_title: CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora
citation: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608
title: BMED 2300 benchmark corpus and evaluation harness for course-grounded pedagogical video generation
description: A reusable benchmark artifact built from the BMED 2300 Bio-Imaging course, packaged with "twenty-three lectures, 1,116 slides, aligned transcripts, a multi-repetition LLM-judge rubric, and regex-grounded objective metrics." Chunks are slide-granular, each embedding preserving a one-to-one link between a textual explanation and its slide image, stored in a flat inner-product FAISS index with 3,072-dimensional vectors. The harness pairs repeated LLM-judge rubric scoring (1-5 scale, n=3 reps) with deterministic metrics such as Flesch reading ease and regex counts of analogies and retrieval prompts.
requirements: Slide-granular chunking so each retrieved record links a textual explanation to a specific slide image
A course corpus with transcripts and slide images so the FAISS index can be rebuilt deterministically
constraints: Out-of-corpus topics fall back to placeholder slides and lose the benefit of course-grounded visual reuse
target_learning_goals: biomedical imaging concepts such as filtered back projection, MRI relaxation, ultrasound transducers, X-ray attenuation, and CT reconstruction artifacts
examples: The corpus was used to evaluate five in-corpus topics with one learner persona, producing ten videos scored by the judge and objective harnesses
key_sources: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608

article_title: Association of completing an intercalated year-long research degree with post-graduation academic success.
citation: Al-Busaidi Ibrahim S., Ju William, Alamri Yassar, Wilkinson Tim J. (2025). Association of completing an intercalated year-long research degree with post-graduation academic success. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07133-7
title: BMedSc(Hons) intercalated research degree at the University of Otago
description: The BMedSc(Hons) is a year-long intercalated honours research degree embedded in the University of Otago's six-year MBChB program, in which students "briefly suspend their normal training to pursue a focused research topic" and submit a thesis. It is offered only to students who have completed three or more years of the MBChB, taken after the third year (more common) or fifth year. The study evaluated its long-term academic outcomes against matched controls.
requirements: Students must have completed three or more years of the MBChB degree to enrol
Award requires submission of a thesis on the research topic
constraints: The study's findings are based on this single program in New Zealand and may not generalize to other countries with differing degree structures
target_learners: Medical students who have completed at least three years of the MBChB program
target_learning_goals: Research experience and training in a field of medical science
examples: 94 graduates from 1995–2006 cohorts were analysed, with a median follow-up of 14.4 years from graduation; 38.3% of cases had published their BMedSc(Hons) projects.
key_sources: Al-Busaidi Ibrahim S., Ju William, Alamri Yassar, Wilkinson Tim J. (2025). Association of completing an intercalated year-long research degree with post-graduation academic success. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07133-7

article_title: Construction of research feedback experimental teaching mode for medical undergraduate students and comparative study with traditional experimental teaching mode.
citation: Miao Chenggui, Huang Yurong, Duan Qiangjun, Mao Yanmei, Chen Jiaqing, Li Yanping, Xia Aixin, Song Yinqiu, Wang Bing. (2025). Construction of research feedback experimental teaching mode for medical undergraduate students and comparative study with traditional experimental teaching mode. BMC Medical Education 25:961. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07538-4
title: BMESA: an eight-objective basic medical experimental skills assessment with 100 points per objective
description: The basic medical experimental skills assessment (BMESA) is the outcome measure aligned with RFETM: 'The BMESA reflected students’ mastery of experimental principles, steps, problem analysis, and experimental skills, and evaluated the improvement of students’ innovative ability.' It has eight assessment objectives, from mastery of scientific research project design to mastery of paper writing, and 'The total score for each assessment objective was 100 points'.
requirements: Developed by a team of professors from the college with the participation of experimental guidance teachers from the college's experimental (practical) teaching center
target_learning_goals: experimental principles, steps, problem analysis, and experimental skills
examples: Each student was assessed for 10 min after the BMESA was completed, with evaluation indicators formulated by the college's professors and executed by the experimental guidance teachers.
key_sources: Miao Chenggui, Huang Yurong, Duan Qiangjun, Mao Yanmei, Chen Jiaqing, Li Yanping, Xia Aixin, Song Yinqiu, Wang Bing. (2025). Construction of research feedback experimental teaching mode for medical undergraduate students and comparative study with traditional experimental teaching mode. BMC Medical Education 25:961. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07538-4

article_title: BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study.
citation: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819
title: Schools wishing to assess scientific knowledge independently of A-levels may find BMAT Section 2 useful, but should not expect it to add predictive value over prior attainment
description: The article's practical recommendation is that institutions wanting a standardised measure of scientific knowledge that does not rely on prior educational attainment may use BMAT Section 2 ('scientific knowledge and applications'), the only section with a consistent pattern of predictive validity for written assessments across both studied institutions. The authors state: "Schools who wish to assess scientific knowledge, independently of A‐levels, may find Section 2 useful." However, this recommendation is bounded by the finding that Section 2 added little over A-level grades.
requirements: Institutions must accept that the predictive utility applies to written assessments and does not extend clearly to clinical assessments or add incremental validity over A-level grades.
constraints: The article found no clear incremental validity of any BMAT section over attained A-level scores.
Associations with clinical assessment performance were absent or negative.
target_learning_goals: selection of applicants likely to perform well on written science-based medical school assessments
examples: The study tested this by regressing BMAT Section 2 scores on written and clinical assessment performance across all programme years at ICSM and LKCMedicine, and by re-running the regressions adjusting for A-level scores.
key_sources: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819

article_title: BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study.
citation: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819
title: BioMedical Admissions Test (BMAT): a three-section admissions test used by more than 40 medical schools globally
description: The BMAT is a medical school admissions test introduced in 2000 at the University of Cambridge, positioned as assessing "academic readiness for demanding science‐based study, not fitness to practise". "It comprises three sections": Section 1 ('thinking skills') measures "skills in ‘problem‐solving, argument comprehension, data and graphical interpretation and inference’"; Section 2 assesses knowledge of core mathematics, biology, chemistry and physics to age-16 qualification level; Section 3 is a 30-minute writing task scored for content (3a) and written English (3b). This study evaluated the predictive and incremental validity of Sections 1, 2 and 3a.
requirements: Used as one component of a medical school selection process alongside prior educational attainment and interviews.
constraints: Section 3b showed very limited variability in these cohorts (76.0% of ICSM students scored the maximum 5 points; 100% of LKCMedicine students scored 5) and was excluded from analysis.
target_learning_goals: standardised assessment of applicants' thinking skills, scientific knowledge and writing for selection decisions
examples: The study analysed BMAT Section 1, Section 2 and Section 3a scores from four ICSM cohorts (2010–2013 entrants) and three LKCMedicine cohorts (2013–2015 entrants).
key_sources: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819

article_title: Student perspectives on barriers to performance for black and minority ethnic graduate-entry medical students: a qualitative study in a West Midlands medical school.
citation: Morrison Nariell, Machado Michelle, Blackburn Clare. (2019). Student perspectives on barriers to performance for black and minority ethnic graduate-entry medical students: a qualitative study in a West Midlands medical school. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-032493
title: Three-theme taxonomy of perceived barriers to performance for BME graduate-entry medical students
description: The study organises BME graduate-entry students' narrated barriers to performance into three main causal themes: importance of relationships (with peers and staff), institution and learning (interactions with the institution and learning opportunities such as patient encounters), and psychosocial and identity factors (stereotyping, racism, cultural differences). Within these, "seven subthemes were identified that were perceived to cause barriers to performance", with relationships with staff and clinicians linked to two main themes and experiences of racism linked across several subthemes.
requirements: Emergent themes depend on the chosen sample; other themes may arise with different or more participants
constraints: Derived from one West Midlands medical school with 24 volunteer and snowball-sampled participants; generalisability not established
target_learners: graduate-entry medical students from BME backgrounds
target_learning_goals: understanding and addressing differential attainment by ethnicity in medical education
examples: Figure 2 maps the main themes and subthemes, including dotted links showing how experiences of racism connect to subthemes in two main themes
key_sources: Morrison Nariell, Machado Michelle, Blackburn Clare. (2019). Student perspectives on barriers to performance for black and minority ethnic graduate-entry medical students: a qualitative study in a West Midlands medical school. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-032493
